content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Across all three blind responses, 'works' are a person's deeds or outward conduct that express and evidence the inner spiritual condition: good works are the fruit of faith/grace (obedience, love, mercy), evil works the fruit of the flesh, unbelief, or darkness; works serve as evidence at judgment. Contested points are soteriological (evidential vs. cooperative role in justification) and the referent of Paul's 'works of the law,' not the basic identification of works as deeds manifesting the heart.","book_summary":"The book identifies works as deeds but explicitly denies that 'works' is a synonym for obedience: a deed only becomes obedience when it executes God's command, and becomes disobedience when another lawgiver governs it (cf. Micah 6:16, works of the house of Ahab under Omri's statutes). Paul's Romans 4 'works' is the laborer's work offered for wage/debt; James 2's work is Abraham's faith made visible. Even complete obedience earns no wage — the servant has only done his duty (Luke 17:7-10). The book thereby rejects the common framing in which Paul's 'works' broadly means human obedience/effort set against faith.","consensus_core_identification":"Works = a person's deeds/actions, functioning as the outward fruit and evidence of the inner condition (good works from faith/grace, evil works from sin/the flesh), and the basis of assessment at judgment.","book_core_identification":"Works = deeds as such, distinct from obedience; a deed is classified as obedience or disobedience by which lawgiver's command governs it, and Paul's polemical 'works' target wage-earning labor offered for debt rather than obedience or effort generally.","core_relation":"COMPATIBLE_OVERLAP","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The consensus (and the book's own common-view note) treats 'works' in Paul as broadly including human obedience and moral effort set against faith, with good works then following as fruit/evidence. The book redraws two boundaries: (1) it severs works from obedience — a work is not inherently obedient or moral; its status depends on whose command governs it (Micah 6:16's evil works are deeds executing Omri's/Ahab's statutes) — so 'evil works' are reclassified from 'deeds of the flesh revealing unbelief' to 'deeds governed by another lawgiver'; (2) it narrows the Pauline works-vs-faith contrast to wage-seeking labor (Rom 4:4-5), excluding obedience itself from Paul's target, and adds that even complete obedience earns no wage (Luke 17:10), removing obedience from the merit/wage economy the consensus's 'works-righteousness' framing presupposes.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"Both readings identify works as human deeds, so the central referent is intact — this is not replacement. But the book materially changes conditions and extension: it denies the works=obedience equivalence that underlies the consensus's fruit/evidence and effort-vs-faith framings, reclassifies evil works by governing lawgiver rather than by inner corruption, and restricts Paul's contested 'works' to wage-oriented labor while insisting obedience earns nothing. These are genuine boundary and classification disagreements within the same category of 'deeds,' fitting REFINED rather than DIVERGENT (no claim that works are something other than deeds) or NOVEL (its Romans 4 move resembles, though it is distinct from, the listed 'works of the law' alternatives).","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue the book's move is closer to MATCH: the consensus also says deeds can be good or evil depending on alignment with God, and 'governed by another lawgiver' is arguably just a restatement of 'fruit of darkness/the devil' (John 8:44; Eph 5:11). On that reading the book's 'not a synonym for obedience' is a terminological sharpening rather than a material reclassification, and its Romans 4 wage-labor reading falls within the already-listed 'works of the law' alternatives.","confidence":"medium"}
